title: AWS: Cloud Practitioner Services and Terms
description: For Cloud Practitioner learners: core AWS services, security responsibilities, architecture, operations, and cost concepts. Examples emphasize service selection; confirm current exam scope and product details in AWS documentation.

sources.name: AWS Overview whitepaper
sources.license: Copyright Amazon Web Services; reference, original definitions

sources.name: AWS Shared Responsibility Model
sources.license: Copyright Amazon Web Services; reference, original explanations

cards.back: On-demand access to computing resources through networked services, with usage-based provisioning and consumption.
cards.example: Rent computing capacity instead of purchasing a server for every workload.

cards.back: The ability to increase or decrease a system's capacity to handle workload changes.
cards.example: Add servers when the user base grows.

cards.back: Adjusting provisioned resources to match changing demand, often automatically.
cards.example: Scale out for a traffic peak and scale in afterward.

cards.back: Designing a system to remain usable despite failures by reducing single points of failure.
cards.example: Run an application across multiple Availability Zones.

cards.back: Continuing to operate through failures, often using redundant components and automatic recovery.
cards.example: A failed component does not stop the overall service.

cards.front: What is agility in the cloud?
cards.back: The ability to provision, test, and change resources quickly.
cards.example: Create a temporary development environment in minutes.

cards.back: A cost that changes with consumption, contrasted with a large fixed upfront investment.
cards.example: Pay for metered compute usage.

cards.back: Lower per-unit costs that can result from operating at large scale.
cards.example: A cloud provider spreads infrastructure costs across many customers.

cards.front: What is Infrastructure as a Service?
cards.back: A model providing basic compute, networking, and storage while customers manage operating systems and applications.
cards.example: Run your own operating system configuration on virtual machines.

cards.front: What is Platform as a Service?
cards.back: A model managing more of the application platform so customers focus on code and data.
cards.example: Deploy application code to a managed runtime platform.

cards.front: What is Software as a Service?
cards.back: A model delivering a finished application operated by a provider.
cards.example: Use a hosted collaboration application through a browser.

cards.back: Cloud infrastructure offered by a provider to multiple customers with logical isolation.
cards.example: Use AWS services in an AWS Region.

cards.back: An architecture combining cloud resources with on-premises or other privately operated environments.
cards.example: Connect a local data center to AWS.

cards.back: Use of cloud services from more than one cloud provider.
cards.example: Operate different workloads across two providers.

cards.back: A geographic area containing multiple Availability Zones.
cards.example: Choose a Region near users and meeting data-location requirements.

cards.back: One or more discrete data centers with redundant infrastructure, isolated from other zones in a Region.
cards.example: Spread instances across zones for resilience.

cards.back: A site used by services such as CloudFront to serve users closer to their location.
cards.example: Cache website content near viewers.

cards.back: AWS infrastructure extensions that place selected services near particular population or industry centers.
cards.example: Place a latency-sensitive workload nearer a city.

cards.back: AWS-managed infrastructure installed at a customer site to run supported AWS services locally.
cards.example: Keep selected workloads on premises while using AWS APIs.

cards.front: What is the shared responsibility model?
cards.back: AWS secures the cloud infrastructure; customers secure their data, identities, configurations, and other responsibilities that depend on the service.
cards.example: On EC2, customers normally patch the guest operating system.

cards.front: What is security of the cloud?
cards.back: AWS's responsibility for protecting the infrastructure that runs AWS services.
cards.example: AWS controls physical access to its data centers.

cards.front: What is security in the cloud?
cards.back: Customer responsibilities that vary with service choice, including permissions, data protection, and workload configuration.
cards.example: A customer chooses who can read its S3 objects.

cards.back: A service providing configurable virtual server instances.
cards.example: Run software that needs control over the guest operating system.

cards.front: What is an Amazon Machine Image?
cards.back: A template containing the software configuration needed to launch an EC2 instance.
cards.example: Launch several instances from an approved base image.

cards.front: What is an EC2 instance type?
cards.back: A hardware configuration class defining compute, memory, storage, and networking characteristics.
cards.example: Choose a memory-optimized type for a memory-heavy workload.

cards.back: Paying for eligible instance usage without a long-term usage commitment.
cards.example: Run an unpredictable short-term workload.

cards.back: Discounted spare EC2 capacity that AWS can interrupt when capacity is needed.
cards.example: Run restartable batch jobs with checkpointing.

cards.back: A billing benefit for matching instance usage in exchange for a term commitment; capacity effects depend on scope and offering.
cards.example: Reduce the cost of a stable eligible EC2 workload.

cards.back: Discounted eligible usage in exchange for a committed amount of usage cost per hour over a term.
cards.example: Commit to a steady baseline of qualifying compute usage.

cards.front: What is an EC2 Dedicated Host?
cards.back: A physical server allocated to a customer, with host-level placement and visibility.
cards.example: Meet some server-bound software licensing requirements.

cards.back: Instances running on hardware dedicated to one customer account, without the same host management controls as Dedicated Hosts.
cards.example: Use single-customer hardware tenancy.

cards.front: What is an On-Demand Capacity Reservation?
cards.back: A reservation of EC2 capacity in a specific Availability Zone for matching instance attributes.
cards.example: Secure capacity for a planned launch without assuming it includes a pricing discount.

cards.front: What is Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling?
cards.back: A service that manages instance group size and replaces unhealthy instances based on configured policies.
cards.example: Add instances when demand increases.

cards.front: What is an Auto Scaling group?
cards.back: A managed collection of EC2 instances with minimum, maximum, and desired capacity settings.
cards.example: Keep a desired number of application instances running.

cards.back: A service family that distributes incoming traffic across registered targets.
cards.example: Send requests to healthy application instances.

cards.front: What is an Application Load Balancer?
cards.back: A load balancer operating at the application layer, supporting HTTP and HTTPS routing rules.
cards.example: Route /images requests to a separate target group.

cards.front: What is a Network Load Balancer?
cards.back: A load balancer designed for transport-layer traffic such as TCP, UDP, and TLS.
cards.example: Distribute low-latency network connections.

cards.back: An event-driven compute service that executes functions without customers managing the underlying servers.
cards.example: Process an object after it is uploaded.

cards.back: A model in which the provider manages server provisioning and much of the operational infrastructure; servers still exist.
cards.example: Run a Lambda function in response to an event.

cards.back: An event source or integration that causes a function to run.
cards.example: An S3 object-created event invokes a function.

cards.back: A managed service for deploying and orchestrating containers.
cards.example: Run a containerized application as ECS tasks and services.

cards.back: A managed Kubernetes service.
cards.example: Run Kubernetes workloads with an AWS-managed control plane.

cards.back: Managed compute capacity for supported container workloads without managing the underlying server fleet.
cards.example: Run ECS tasks without operating EC2 worker instances.

cards.back: A container image registry integrated with AWS identity and deployment services.
cards.example: Store a versioned application container image.

cards.back: An application deployment service that provisions and manages supporting resources for supported application platforms.
cards.example: Deploy web application code onto a managed environment.

cards.back: A simplified cloud platform with bundled resources for common small application needs.
cards.example: Launch a straightforward virtual private server website.

cards.back: A service that schedules and runs batch computing jobs using configured compute resources.
cards.example: Process a large queue of independent analysis jobs.

cards.back: Object storage that stores data as objects inside buckets.
cards.example: Store images, backups, or data-lake files.

cards.back: A container for objects and their associated configuration in Amazon S3.
cards.example: Create a bucket for application uploads.

cards.back: Data stored with a key and metadata in a bucket.
cards.example: An uploaded photograph is an object.

cards.front: What is an S3 object key?
cards.back: The name identifying an object within a bucket.
cards.example: photos/summer.jpg identifies one object.

cards.back: A bucket feature that retains multiple versions of objects.
cards.example: Recover an earlier object version after an overwrite.

cards.front: What is an S3 Lifecycle rule?
cards.back: A policy that transitions or expires objects based on defined conditions.
cards.example: Move older data to an archival storage class.

cards.back: An S3 storage class for frequently accessed data with multi-AZ resilience.
cards.example: Serve frequently requested application assets.

cards.back: A multi-AZ storage class for infrequently accessed data requiring rapid access, with retrieval-related charges.
cards.example: Retain a rarely accessed backup that must be retrieved quickly.

cards.back: A lower-cost infrequent-access class that stores data in one Availability Zone.
cards.example: Store reproducible data that can tolerate loss of a zone.

cards.back: A storage class that can move objects among access tiers based on access patterns, with applicable monitoring and tier rules.
cards.example: Store data whose access frequency is hard to predict.

cards.front: What is S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval?
cards.back: An archival storage class providing millisecond access for rarely accessed data, with its own pricing conditions.
cards.example: Retrieve an archived image immediately when needed.

cards.front: What is S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval?
cards.back: An archive storage class with retrieval options that generally require a restore process and waiting time.
cards.example: Restore archived files when immediate access is unnecessary.

cards.front: What is S3 Glacier Deep Archive?
cards.back: An S3 class for long-lived, very rarely retrieved data with longer restore times.
cards.example: Retain a long-term archive that can wait for retrieval.

cards.front: What is S3 Block Public Access?
cards.back: Controls that help prevent public access through supported bucket and access-point settings and policies.
cards.example: Reduce the risk of accidentally public data.

cards.back: Persistent block storage volumes used with EC2 and other supported integrations.
cards.example: Attach a data disk to an EC2 instance.

cards.back: A point-in-time backup of an EBS volume managed by AWS.
cards.example: Restore a volume from an earlier snapshot.

cards.back: Temporary block storage physically attached to the host, with lifecycle-dependent persistence.
cards.example: Use it for disposable cache data.

cards.back: Managed elastic NFS file storage for supported clients.
cards.example: Share files across Linux application instances.

cards.back: A family of managed file systems built around specific file-system technologies.
cards.example: Choose FSx for Windows File Server for an SMB workload.

cards.back: Hybrid storage services that connect on-premises environments with cloud-backed storage.
cards.example: Give local applications access to cloud-backed storage interfaces.

cards.back: A service for centrally managing backup policies and recovery points across supported resources.
cards.example: Apply a scheduled backup plan to several resource types.

cards.back: A service for moving data between supported storage locations with managed transfer operations.
cards.example: Transfer file data from a local system to AWS storage.

cards.back: Managed file-transfer interfaces using supported protocols such as SFTP with AWS storage back ends.
cards.example: Let a partner upload files using SFTP.

cards.back: A managed relational database service that handles many infrastructure and database administration tasks.
cards.example: Run a managed PostgreSQL database.

cards.back: An AWS relational database engine compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, with a distributed storage design.
cards.example: Use an Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible database.

cards.back: A managed serverless key-value and document database.
cards.example: Store application items keyed by a customer identifier.

cards.back: Managed in-memory caching and data-store capabilities for supported engines.
cards.example: Cache frequently read results to reduce database load.

cards.back: A managed analytics data warehouse for querying large structured datasets.
cards.example: Analyze historical business metrics with SQL.

cards.back: A managed graph database service.
cards.example: Query relationships among entities in a graph.

cards.back: A managed document database service offering MongoDB API compatibility for supported operations.
cards.example: Store and query document-oriented application data.

cards.front: What is Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployment?
cards.back: An RDS deployment approach using multiple Availability Zones to improve availability; details depend on the deployment type.
cards.example: Fail over after an infrastructure problem in one zone.

cards.front: What is an RDS read replica?
cards.back: A database replica primarily used to serve read traffic; capabilities vary by database engine.
cards.example: Offload reporting reads from the primary database.

cards.back: A database organizing data in related tables, commonly queried with SQL.
cards.example: Join customers and orders by an identifier.

cards.back: A database that retrieves values using associated keys.
cards.example: Look up a session record by session ID.

cards.back: A faster storage layer holding copies or derived results to reduce repeated work.
cards.example: Reuse a recent database query result.

cards.back: A logically isolated virtual network for AWS resources.
cards.example: Define address ranges, subnets, routes, and traffic controls.

cards.back: A range of IP addresses within a VPC; an AWS subnet resides in one Availability Zone.
cards.example: Place application instances in a private subnet.

cards.back: A subnet whose route table includes a route to an internet gateway; individual resource access also requires appropriate addressing and permissions.
cards.example: A public-facing resource needs more than just public-subnet placement.

cards.back: A subnet without a direct route to an internet gateway.
cards.example: Place a backend database away from direct internet access.

cards.back: A set of rules determining where network traffic is directed.
cards.example: Send internet-bound traffic to the appropriate gateway.

cards.back: A VPC component enabling internet connectivity for appropriately configured resources.
cards.example: Provide a public subnet with a route to the internet.

cards.front: What is a public NAT gateway?
cards.back: A managed gateway typically allowing private IPv4 resources to initiate outbound internet connections without accepting unsolicited inbound connections.
cards.example: Download updates from a private subnet.

cards.back: A stateful virtual firewall controlling traffic for associated resources using allow rules.
cards.example: Permit HTTPS to an application instance.

cards.back: A stateless subnet-level traffic filter with allow and deny rules.
cards.example: Restrict a subnet's inbound and outbound traffic separately.

cards.back: A way to privately reach supported services without relying on an internet gateway for that traffic.
cards.example: Access S3 through a supported VPC endpoint.

cards.back: Private connectivity to supported services using endpoints and AWS networking.
cards.example: Consume an endpoint service without exposing it publicly.

cards.back: A private routing connection between two VPCs; it is not transitive by default.
cards.example: Connect two application networks directly.

cards.back: A network hub connecting VPCs and on-premises networks.
cards.example: Centralize routing among many VPCs.

cards.back: An encrypted network connection between a customer network and AWS over IPsec tunnels.
cards.example: Connect a branch network to a VPC.

cards.back: A dedicated network connection from a customer location to AWS; encryption is not inherent in every configuration.
cards.example: Use a dedicated connectivity path to AWS.

cards.back: An AWS DNS service with capabilities including domain registration, routing policies, and health checks.
cards.example: Map a domain name to an application endpoint.

cards.back: A content delivery network that caches and serves content through distributed edge locations.
cards.example: Deliver static website assets near users.

cards.back: A networking service using static anycast IP addresses and the AWS global network to direct supported traffic to endpoints.
cards.example: Improve paths to a multi-Region application.

cards.back: A service for creating, publishing, securing, and managing APIs.
cards.example: Expose an HTTPS API backed by Lambda.

cards.back: Identity and Access Management, which controls who can perform which actions on which AWS resources.
cards.example: Grant a role permission to read a specific bucket.

cards.back: An identity in an AWS account that can have permissions and credentials.
cards.example: A legacy integration might use an IAM user, though roles and temporary credentials are preferred when possible.

cards.back: An assumable identity providing temporary permissions without requiring long-lived user credentials.
cards.example: An EC2 workload assumes a role to access S3.

cards.back: A document defining permission statements for AWS actions and resources.
cards.example: Allow GetObject on a designated bucket's objects.

cards.front: What is the principle of least privilege?
cards.back: Granting only the permissions needed for the required task.
cards.example: Give a reader read access without delete access.

cards.front: What is AWS account root user?
cards.back: The identity with complete access to an account, reserved for tasks requiring it and protected carefully.
cards.example: Use strong authentication and avoid routine root use.

cards.back: Authentication requiring more than one independent factor.
cards.example: Combine a password with a security key or authenticator.

cards.front: What is AWS IAM Identity Center?
cards.back: Centralized workforce access management for multiple AWS accounts and supported applications.
cards.example: Provide employees federated access through assigned permission sets.

cards.back: Using a trusted external identity system to obtain access to another system.
cards.example: Employees sign in with a corporate identity provider.

cards.back: Security Token Service, which issues temporary security credentials.
cards.example: Assume a role for a time-limited session.

cards.back: A service for centrally managing multiple AWS accounts.
cards.example: Group accounts into organizational units.

cards.front: What is a service control policy?
cards.back: An Organizations policy setting permission boundaries for member accounts; it does not grant permissions by itself.
cards.example: Prevent member accounts from using disallowed actions.

cards.back: A grouping of accounts within AWS Organizations for management and policy application.
cards.example: Apply common guardrails to development accounts.

cards.back: A service that helps establish and govern a multi-account AWS environment.
cards.example: Set up a landing zone with baseline controls.

cards.back: A service for managing cryptographic keys and performing integrated cryptographic operations.
cards.example: Control a key used to encrypt service data.

cards.back: A service providing dedicated hardware security modules for customer-controlled cryptographic operations.
cards.example: Use an HSM for a specialized key-management requirement.

cards.back: A service for securely storing and retrieving secrets, with supported rotation workflows.
cards.example: Store database credentials outside application code.

cards.back: A service for provisioning and managing supported TLS certificates.
cards.example: Attach a managed certificate to an HTTPS endpoint.

cards.back: A web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests using configured rules.
cards.example: Block a known malicious request pattern.

cards.back: Managed protection against distributed denial-of-service attacks, with Standard and Advanced offerings.
cards.example: Protect supported public-facing resources from DDoS threats.

cards.back: A threat-detection service analyzing supported data sources for suspicious activity.
cards.example: Investigate unusual account or workload behavior.

cards.back: A vulnerability-management service for supported workloads and software.
cards.example: Find known vulnerabilities in supported deployed packages.

cards.back: A service that helps discover and protect sensitive data in S3.
cards.example: Identify objects containing potentially sensitive information.

cards.back: A service that centralizes supported security findings and security posture information.
cards.example: Review findings from several security services together.

cards.back: A portal providing access to AWS compliance reports and selected agreements.
cards.example: Download an applicable audit report for review.

cards.back: Identity capabilities for adding user sign-up, sign-in, and access flows to applications.
cards.example: Authenticate users of a consumer web application.

cards.back: A monitoring and observability service for metrics, logs, alarms, and related telemetry.
cards.example: Alarm when an application's error rate rises.
cards.hint: Think of operational metrics, logs, and alarms.

cards.back: A rule that evaluates a metric or expression and changes state based on configured thresholds.
cards.example: Notify an operator about high CPU utilization.

cards.back: A service recording AWS account activity and API events for auditing and investigation.
cards.example: Review who changed a resource's configuration.
cards.hint: Think of account activity and API auditing.

cards.back: A service recording supported resource configurations and evaluating them against rules.
cards.example: Check whether a resource matches a desired configuration.

cards.back: A suite for managing and operating supported infrastructure at scale.
cards.example: Run controlled maintenance actions on managed nodes.

cards.back: A service providing checks and recommendations across areas such as cost, performance, and security, with access depending on support arrangements.
cards.example: Review a recommendation about unused resources.

cards.back: Information about AWS service events and account-relevant operational issues.
cards.example: Check whether a service event affects your resources.

cards.back: A service that provisions and manages infrastructure from templates.
cards.example: Create a repeatable application stack.

cards.back: A collection of resources managed as one unit through CloudFormation.
cards.example: Update a network and its associated resources together.

cards.back: A software development framework for defining cloud infrastructure in supported programming languages, commonly synthesized into CloudFormation templates.
cards.example: Define an infrastructure construct in TypeScript.

cards.back: Managing infrastructure through versioned machine-readable definitions.
cards.example: Review an infrastructure change in source control.

cards.back: A tool for exploring historical costs and usage and generating forecasts.
cards.example: Find which service drove a spending increase.

cards.back: A service for tracking costs or usage against configured budgets and taking supported actions or sending alerts.
cards.example: Notify a team when spending approaches its budget.

cards.back: A tool for estimating AWS costs from an intended resource configuration.
cards.example: Model the expected cost of a proposed architecture.

cards.back: Resource tags activated for supported cost categorization and reporting.
cards.example: Report spending by project tag.

cards.back: Combining charges for accounts in an organization under a management account's bill.
cards.example: Review a combined bill for multiple accounts.

cards.back: A service that recommends resource configurations based on supported utilization data.
cards.example: Identify an oversized compute resource.

cards.back: Matching resource capacity and configuration to actual workload needs.
cards.example: Reduce an oversized instance after reviewing metrics.

cards.back: An account, Region, or resource limit for a service, with some quotas adjustable.
cards.example: Request an increase before a large deployment.

cards.back: Support offerings that provide varying access to technical help and guidance.
cards.example: Use the applicable support channel for an operational issue.

cards.back: Guidance for evaluating cloud workloads across six architectural pillars.
cards.example: Review a workload for reliability and cost concerns.

cards.front: What is the Operational Excellence pillar?
cards.back: Guidance on running, monitoring, learning from, and improving systems and processes.
cards.example: Improve incident response through documented procedures.

cards.back: Guidance on protecting data, systems, identities, and assets.
cards.example: Apply least privilege and prepare for security events.

cards.back: Guidance on correct operation, recovery, and adaptation to changing demand or failure.
cards.example: Test recovery from an Availability Zone outage.

cards.front: What is the Performance Efficiency pillar?
cards.back: Guidance on using computing resources efficiently as requirements and technologies change.
cards.example: Choose an appropriate database and instance family.

cards.front: What is the Cost Optimization pillar?
cards.back: Guidance on delivering business value while avoiding unnecessary expense.
cards.example: Remove idle resources and measure unit cost.

cards.back: Guidance on reducing the environmental impact of cloud workloads.
cards.example: Improve utilization and reduce unnecessary processing.

cards.front: What is a recovery time objective?
cards.back: The target maximum acceptable time to restore a workload after disruption.
cards.example: A service may target recovery within one hour.

cards.front: What is a recovery point objective?
cards.back: The target maximum acceptable data-loss interval measured backward from a disruption.
cards.example: A five-minute objective requires sufficiently frequent recoverable data updates.

cards.back: A recoverable copy of data retained to restore after loss or corruption.
cards.example: Restore a deleted database from a backup.

cards.back: Maintaining copies of data across locations or resources.
cards.example: Replicate data to support availability, while recognizing that replication alone may copy corruption.

cards.back: Planning and implementing restoration after a major disruptive event.
cards.example: Test recovery of an application in an alternate location.

cards.back: A managed message queue service for asynchronous communication.
cards.example: Buffer jobs between a producer and worker fleet.

cards.back: A publish-subscribe messaging service that delivers messages to subscribed endpoints.
cards.example: Send one event to multiple subscribers.

cards.back: A service for routing events from supported sources to targets using event rules and related capabilities.
cards.example: Route an application event to a processing workflow.

cards.back: A workflow orchestration service using state machines and service integrations.
cards.example: Coordinate several tasks with retries and branching.

cards.back: A queue holding messages that could not be processed successfully under configured delivery rules.
cards.example: Inspect a repeatedly failing task message.

cards.back: Designing components to interact through limited interfaces rather than tight dependencies.
cards.example: Insert a queue between request ingestion and processing.

cards.front: What is Amazon Kinesis Data Streams?
cards.back: A service for collecting and processing ordered data streams within shards.
cards.example: Ingest a continuous stream of application events.

cards.back: A serverless query service commonly used to analyze data in S3 with SQL.
cards.example: Query log files without operating a database server.

cards.back: A data integration service with cataloging and extract-transform-load capabilities.
cards.example: Prepare datasets for analytics and catalog their schemas.

cards.back: A managed platform for big-data processing with frameworks such as Apache Spark.
cards.example: Run distributed analytics jobs.

cards.back: A repository holding large amounts of data in varied formats for later processing and analysis.
cards.example: Store raw structured and unstructured data in S3.

cards.back: A managed service for search and analytics using supported OpenSearch-related capabilities.
cards.example: Index logs for interactive search.

cards.back: A managed service for building generative AI applications using supported foundation models and related tools.
cards.example: Call a foundation model through a managed service API.

cards.back: An image and video analysis service with supported computer-vision features.
cards.example: Detect objects in an image.

cards.back: A natural-language processing service for extracting information from text.
cards.example: Identify entities or sentiment in a document.

cards.back: A service that converts text into speech.
cards.example: Generate spoken audio from written content.

cards.back: A service that converts speech into text.
cards.example: Produce a transcript from recorded audio.

cards.back: A service for machine translation between supported languages.
cards.example: Translate application text for users.

cards.back: A service that extracts text and structured information from supported documents.
cards.example: Read form fields and tables from a scanned document.

cards.back: Database Migration Service, used to migrate and replicate data between supported database sources and targets.
cards.example: Move a database while reducing migration downtime.

cards.front: What is AWS Application Migration Service?
cards.back: A service supporting lift-and-shift migration of servers to AWS.
cards.example: Replicate a server and launch it as an EC2 workload.

cards.back: A place to track and coordinate supported migration activities.
cards.example: Monitor progress across a migration project.

cards.back: A managed service that runs software build and test jobs.
cards.example: Compile an application without maintaining a build server.

cards.back: A service for modeling and automating release pipelines.
cards.example: Run build and deployment stages after a source change.

cards.back: A service that automates application deployments to supported compute targets.
cards.example: Roll out a new application version.

cards.back: A browser-accessible shell with AWS tools and an authenticated environment.
cards.example: Run an AWS CLI command from the console.

cards.back: A command-line interface for calling AWS service APIs.
cards.example: List resources from a shell script.

cards.back: A language-specific library for interacting with AWS service APIs.
cards.example: Use a Python library to call S3.

cards.front: What is the AWS Management Console?
cards.back: A web interface for managing AWS services and resources.
cards.example: Inspect an EC2 instance in a browser.

cards.front: What is an AWS resource tag?
cards.back: A key-value label attached to supported resources for organization and automation.
cards.example: Label a resource with its project name.

cards.back: Protection of stored data using cryptographic encoding.
cards.example: Encrypt a stored volume.

cards.back: Protection of data while it travels between endpoints.
cards.example: Use TLS for an HTTPS connection.

cards.front: What is a stateless application tier?
cards.back: A tier that does not rely on a particular server retaining client session state locally between requests.
cards.example: Store session state externally so another instance can handle the next request.

cards.back: A probe or assessment used to determine whether a target is functioning as expected.
cards.example: A load balancer stops routing to an unhealthy target.

cards.back: A release method using separate old and new environments and switching traffic between them.
cards.example: Validate the new environment before redirecting production requests.

cards.back: A release method exposing a new version to a small portion of traffic before wider rollout.
cards.example: Monitor a limited rollout before expanding it.

cards.back: Moving a workload with minimal architectural change, often called lift and shift.
cards.example: Move an existing server-based application to EC2.

cards.front: What is refactoring for cloud migration?
cards.back: Changing an application's design to better use cloud capabilities.
cards.example: Replace a tightly coupled component with event-driven processing.

cards.back: Adding or removing parallel resource units, such as application instances, to change capacity.
cards.example: Add two instances behind a load balancer.

cards.back: Changing the capacity of an individual resource, such as moving to an instance with more memory or CPU.
cards.example: Replace a small instance with a larger instance type.

cards.front: What is a single point of failure?
cards.back: A component whose failure alone can stop the required operation of the wider system.
cards.example: One application server with no replacement mechanism can be a single point of failure.
